read_pl.title: Reading the Profit & Loss
read_pl.desc: For managers handed a P&L every month: what each line actually means, why gross margin is the number to watch, which lines carry somebody's judgement, and six questions that turn a statement into a decision. Worked throughout in naira, on retail and distribution numbers.

lessons.title: Revenue: when a sale becomes a sale
lessons.html:
The top line looks like the simplest number on the page and is the one most often misread. Revenue is not the money that arrived in the bank this month. It is the value of what you delivered this month, whenever the customer happens to pay.

Those two things come apart constantly, and in both directions.

A sale with no money. You supply a distributor ₦4,000,000 of stock on thirty days' credit on the 20th. The goods are gone, the invoice is raised, the customer owes you. That ₦4,000,000 is revenue this month even though not one naira has been received, and it will still be revenue if they pay late, pay slowly, or never pay at all.

Money with no sale. A customer pays ₦1,500,000 in advance for goods you will deliver next month. Your bank balance rises today. Your revenue does not. You are holding somebody else's money until you deliver — it sits as a liability, not as income.

Why the rule exists. If revenue followed cash, a manager could make a bad month look good simply by chasing customers hard in the last week, and a good month look poor by letting collections slip. The performance of the business would become a story about collection timing rather than about trading. Recognising revenue on delivery keeps the top line describing what the business actually did.

What this means when you read your own P&L. A rise in revenue tells you that more was delivered. It tells you nothing whatever about whether you were paid, and nothing about whether you will be. Those questions are answered on the balance sheet, under receivables, and in the cash flow statement — which is why a manager who reads only the P&L can watch revenue climb every month while the business quietly runs out of money.

Two things that reduce revenue and are easy to miss. Returns come off the top line, so a month with heavy returns shows lower revenue rather than a separate cost. Trade discounts do the same — a 10% discount on ₦2,000,000 of goods is ₦1,800,000 of revenue, not ₦2,000,000 of revenue and a ₦200,000 cost. That matters when you are trying to work out why margin moved, because discounting hides inside the top line rather than announcing itself.

And one thing that is not revenue at all: VAT. The VAT you charge a customer was never yours. You collect it on behalf of the tax authority and pass it on. A P&L that shows revenue inclusive of VAT overstates the business by that amount, and every margin calculated from it will be wrong. When somebody quotes a revenue figure, it is always worth knowing whether it is gross or net of VAT — the two differ by 7.5% and people quote them interchangeably.

WATCH-OUT: The month a business changes its delivery pattern — a big order shipped on the 30th instead of the 2nd — revenue jumps or falls for reasons that have nothing to do with demand. Before concluding anything from a single month, ask what was delivered and when.

One more thing the top line will not tell you. Revenue says nothing about whether the sale was any good. A month of heavy discounting and a month of full-price trading can produce identical revenue, and only the next line down begins to separate them. Managers who report upward on revenue alone are describing activity rather than performance, which is why the first question any experienced reader asks about a good revenue month is what it cost to get.

checks.q: You deliver ₦4m of goods on 30-day credit on the 20th. Revenue this month is:
opts: ₦4m less an allowance for late payment
checks.why: Revenue follows delivery, not collection. Whether you get paid is a receivables question, answered on the balance sheet.

checks.q: A customer pays ₦1.5m in advance for next month's delivery. This month you record:
opts: No revenue — you are holding their money until you deliver
checks.why: Cash arrived but nothing was delivered. Until it is, the money is a liability, not income.

checks.q: Why does recognising revenue on delivery rather than on payment matter to a manager?
opts: It stops the top line becoming a story about collection timing
checks.why: If revenue followed cash, a hard collection push would flatter a bad month and slow collections would spoil a good one — and neither says anything about trading.

lessons.title: Cost of sales, and what sits inside it
lessons.html:
Cost of sales is what the goods you sold actually cost you. Not what you bought this month, not what is sitting in the warehouse — what went out of the door in the hands of customers.

That distinction is the single most common misreading in a retail P&L, so it is worth being slow about.

Buying is not a cost. When you buy ₦10,000,000 of stock, nothing has happened to your profit. You have swapped one asset, cash, for another asset, inventory. The P&L does not move. Only when you sell those goods does their cost cross into cost of sales.

So a month of heavy buying ahead of a festive peak does not depress profit, though it will certainly depress your bank balance. A manager who confuses the two will report a disaster to a board that is looking at a perfectly healthy P&L, or the reverse.

The arithmetic behind the line. Cost of sales is worked out from what you started with, what you added, and what is left:

Opening stock ₦18,000,000, plus purchases ₦42,000,000, less closing stock ₦21,000,000, gives cost of sales of ₦39,000,000. Everything that came in and did not remain is treated as having been sold.

Notice what that arithmetic quietly does. It assumes that anything missing was sold. It was not necessarily sold — it may have been stolen, broken, expired or miscounted. Shrinkage does not appear as a line called shrinkage; it disappears silently into cost of sales and shows up as a margin that is worse than it should be, with no explanation attached.

This is why a manager investigating a fall in gross margin must always ask whether the stock count was any good. A closing stock figure that is overstated by ₦2,000,000 understates cost of sales by exactly ₦2,000,000 and overstates profit by the same. The P&L will look better and be wrong.

What else belongs in cost of sales. Beyond the purchase price of the goods: inbound freight, clearing and duty on imports, and any direct handling needed to get goods sellable. The test is whether the cost was incurred to get the goods ready to sell. Delivering them to the customer afterwards is a selling cost, not a cost of sale — a distinction worth holding, because moving delivery costs between the two lines changes gross margin without changing profit at all.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: If gross margin moves more than a point or two without a price or supplier change, look at stock before you look at anything else. Count quality, cut-off errors on goods received near month-end, and unrecorded write-offs explain most unexplained margin movements in retail and distribution.

A note on timing at month-end. Goods received on the last day but not entered until the first of the next month, or an invoice posted before the stock physically arrived, both distort the calculation — and both are common precisely because month-end is busy. This is called a cut-off error, and its signature is a margin that looks wrong one month and unusually good the next, as the two errors reverse. If you see that pattern, the trading was probably fine and the paperwork was not.

checks.q: You buy ₦10m of stock in March and sell none of it. The effect on March profit is:
opts: Nothing — you swapped cash for inventory
checks.why: Buying moves value between two assets. Cost only reaches the P&L when the goods are sold.

checks.q: Opening stock ₦18m, purchases ₦42m, closing stock ₦21m. Cost of sales is:
checks.why: 18 + 42 − 21 = 39. Whatever came in and did not remain is treated as sold.

checks.q: Closing stock is overstated by ₦2m because of a bad count. The P&L will show:
opts: No effect — stock is a balance sheet item
checks.why: Overstated closing stock understates cost of sales by the same amount, so profit is flattered by exactly ₦2m.

lessons.title: Gross margin: the number that describes your trading
lessons.html:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of sales, and gross margin is that expressed as a percentage of revenue. On ₦60,000,000 of revenue and ₦39,000,000 of cost of sales, gross profit is ₦21,000,000 and gross margin is 35%.

Of every number on the P&L, this is the one a manager should watch most closely, because it describes the thing the business fundamentally does: buy or make something, and sell it for more.

Margin and markup are not the same number, and confusing them costs real money. Buy at ₦1,000 and sell at ₦1,500. The markup — the uplift on cost — is 50%. The margin — the share of the selling price you keep — is ₦500 ÷ ₦1,500, which is 33%. Anyone who prices for a 40% margin by adding 40% to cost has actually priced a 29% margin and will wonder for months why the numbers never come out.

Why percentage matters more than the naira amount. Gross profit in naira grows simply because you sold more; it tells you about size. Margin tells you about health, and it holds still when volume moves. A business whose gross profit rises 20% while margin falls from 35% to 31% is buying its growth — with discounts, or by shifting toward cheaper products — and that trade may or may not be one anybody chose.

Four things move margin, and they need different responses.

Selling price. Discounting, promotions, and the slow drift that happens when staff have authority to negotiate and nobody watches the average.

Buying price. Supplier increases, currency movement on imported goods, losing a volume rebate. Currency deserves particular attention: goods bought at ₦1,600 to the dollar and repriced at ₦1,500 lose margin that no amount of selling effort recovers.

Mix. Selling proportionally more low-margin lines drags the average down even when no single product's margin changed at all. This is the most commonly missed cause, because every individual product looks fine.

Loss. Shrinkage, damage and expiry, which as we saw arrive silently inside cost of sales.

Reading it well means asking which of the four moved. A margin fall of two points has a completely different remedy depending on the answer: a pricing conversation, a supplier conversation, a merchandising decision, or a stock control investigation. The P&L will not tell you which — but it tells you to go and look, and roughly how much is at stake.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Track gross margin by month as a percentage on one line, for at least twelve months. Almost nothing in a trading business is more informative for the effort, and a drift of half a point a month is invisible in isolation and severe over a year.

What good looks like. A manager who knows their margin knows it as a number they could say aloud without looking — this month, last month, and the same month last year. That sounds like a small thing. It is the difference between noticing a two-point fall in the week it happens and discovering it in a quarterly review, by which point the cause is three months cold and the money is gone.

checks.q: You buy at ₦1,000 and sell at ₦1,500. The gross MARGIN is:
checks.why: Margin is profit as a share of the selling price: 500 ÷ 1,500 = 33%. The 50% figure is markup, on cost.

checks.q: Gross profit rose 20% while gross margin fell from 35% to 31%. This means:
opts: The business bought its growth, with discount or cheaper mix
checks.why: Naira profit tells you about size, margin about health. Growing volume at a worse margin is a trade somebody should have chosen deliberately.

checks.q: Every product's margin is unchanged, yet overall gross margin fell. The most likely cause is:
opts: Mix — proportionally more low-margin lines sold
checks.why: Mix is the commonest missed cause precisely because each product looks fine on its own.

lessons.title: Operating expenses and the fixed-cost base
lessons.html:
Below gross profit sit the costs of running the business rather than of buying the goods: salaries, rent, power, fuel, security, transport, marketing, professional fees, bank charges, software. Together they are operating expenses, and the useful way to read them is not by category but by behaviour.

Fixed costs do not move with sales. Rent is the same in a quiet month. So is the security contract, most salaries, and the ERP subscription.

Variable costs move roughly in proportion to activity: sales commission, transaction fees on card payments, delivery fuel, packaging.

Step costs hold flat and then jump. One supervisor covers a shop up to a point, then you need a second. A generator covers a certain load until you need a bigger one. These are the costs that surprise people, because they behave like fixed costs right up until they do not.

Why the distinction is the most useful thing in this chapter. It tells you what a change in sales does to profit. If a branch carries ₦4,000,000 a month of fixed cost and earns 35% margin, it needs about ₦11,400,000 of revenue simply to cover that base before making a naira. Every additional sale beyond it contributes 35 kobo in the naira almost straight to profit, because the fixed costs are already paid for.

That asymmetry is why a modest fall in sales can wipe out a branch's profit entirely while a modest rise transforms it, and why managers are so often surprised by both.

Reading the expense block on your own P&L. Compare each line to revenue as a percentage, not to last month in naira. Salaries at ₦6,000,000 mean nothing on their own; salaries at 10% of revenue against 8% last year is a finding. Fixed costs rising as a share of revenue is the early signal of a business growing its overhead faster than its trading.

And watch what hides in "sundry" or "general". A line that grows quietly and is never questioned because nobody owns it is where uncontrolled spending accumulates. If any single expense category is large and vaguely named, that is where to look first.

WATCH-OUT: Cutting fixed costs feels decisive and is often the wrong first move. A branch failing to cover a ₦4m base may have a revenue problem rather than a cost problem, and cutting the staff who generate the revenue is how a slow decline becomes a fast one. Establish which side the gap is on before acting.

One line that is neither fixed nor variable in the way people assume: energy. In a Nigerian operation, diesel for the generator moves with hours of grid failure rather than with sales. It looks variable, behaves unpredictably, and is large enough to distort a month. Treat it as its own thing rather than forcing it into either category, and read it against hours run rather than against revenue.

checks.q: Sales commission and card transaction fees are:
checks.why: They move roughly in proportion to activity, which is what makes a cost variable.

checks.q: A branch carries ₦4m monthly fixed cost at 35% gross margin. Revenue needed to cover it:
checks.why: ₦4m ÷ 0.35 ≈ ₦11.4m. Each naira of sales contributes only 35 kobo toward the fixed base.

checks.q: Salaries were ₦6m last year and ₦6m this year. On its own this tells you:
opts: Very little — compare them as a share of revenue
Nothing has changed in the business
checks.why: Flat in naira while revenue grew is a real improvement; flat while revenue fell is a growing problem. The percentage carries the meaning.

lessons.title: Operating profit, net profit, and why both exist
lessons.html:
Below the expense block the P&L gives you profit more than once, and each version answers a different question. Reading the wrong one is how managers end up arguing past each other.

Operating profit is gross profit less operating expenses. It answers: does the trading operation work? It deliberately excludes how the business is financed and what tax it pays, because neither is the operating manager's doing.

Net profit is what remains after interest and tax. It answers: what did the owners actually make?

Why separating them matters, in one example. Two branches each produce ₦8,000,000 of operating profit. One is funded by the owner's own money, the other by a loan costing ₦3,000,000 a year in interest. The second delivers ₦5,000,000 to the owners against the first's ₦8,000,000. As operations they performed identically, and the manager of the second should not be marked down for a financing decision made above them.

The reverse error is equally common: judging a business on operating profit alone while it is being quietly consumed by the cost of its debt.

The line to be careful with is interest. It is not an operating cost and does not belong in a branch's performance, but it is entirely real. A business generating good operating profit and negative net profit does not have a trading problem; it has a financing problem, and no amount of selling harder will fix it.

Where tax sits. Below net profit before tax, and it is worth knowing that the tax charge in the accounts rarely equals the cash paid to the tax authority in the same period. They are computed on different bases and on different timing. For an operating manager this matters mainly as a caution: do not reconcile your tax line to your bank statement and expect them to agree.

Which number should you be held to? Almost always operating profit, and for the reason above — it is the part you control. If you are being measured on net profit, you are being measured partly on decisions somebody else made about borrowing, and that is worth saying out loud before the review rather than during it.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: When somebody quotes "profit" without qualifying it, ask which one. The gap between operating and net profit in a business carrying debt can be most of the number, and two people using the same word for different lines will reach opposite conclusions and both be certain.

A third measure you will meet: EBITDA. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation — operating profit with the non-cash charges added back. It is popular because it approximates cash generated by trading, and it is misused because it flatters any business with heavy assets. It is a useful number for comparing operations; it is not profit, and it is not what the owners keep.

checks.q: Two branches both make ₦8m operating profit; one carries ₦3m of interest. As operations they:
checks.why: Interest is a financing cost, not an operating one. Operating profit deliberately excludes it so trading can be judged on its own.

checks.q: A business with healthy operating profit and negative net profit has:
checks.why: The operation works; the cost of its debt is consuming the result. Selling harder will not fix it.

checks.q: An operating manager should normally be measured on:
checks.why: It is the part they control. Net profit folds in borrowing decisions made above them.

lessons.title: Depreciation and amortisation: cost without payment
lessons.html:
Two lines in the expense block are unlike all the others: no money leaves the business when they are charged. They are the most misunderstood items on the P&L and the reason profit and cash differ even in a business that collects promptly.

What depreciation is doing. You buy delivery vehicles for ₦24,000,000 expected to last five years. Charging the whole ₦24,000,000 against the month you bought them would be absurd — it would report a catastrophic month followed by four years of flattered ones, and none of those numbers would describe the business. Instead the cost is spread across the years the vehicles are used: ₦4,800,000 a year, ₦400,000 a month.

That monthly ₦400,000 is a real cost. The vehicles are genuinely being used up. But no payment accompanies it — the money left the bank when you bought them.

Amortisation is the same idea for things you cannot touch: software licences, development costs, goodwill on an acquisition.

The two consequences a manager must hold on to.

First, profit is not cash, and depreciation is one of the main reasons. A business showing ₦2,000,000 profit with ₦3,000,000 of depreciation generated roughly ₦5,000,000 of cash from trading. This is why the cash flow statement starts with profit and adds depreciation straight back.

Second, depreciation is an estimate, and estimates can flatter. Whoever decides that vehicles last five years rather than three has changed reported profit without anything happening in the real world. Lengthening useful lives is one of the quietest ways to improve a profit figure, and it is entirely legitimate right up until it is not.

What it does not do. Depreciation does not set money aside to replace the asset. Nothing is being saved. When the vehicles need replacing, the business needs cash it may not have — which is why a company can be profitable for five years and then be unable to afford the trucks it depends on.

Where this bites in practice. A distribution business with an ageing fleet reports healthy profit for years while its vehicles quietly reach the end of their lives. The replacement bill arrives all at once, has to be funded from cash or borrowing, and the business that looked profitable throughout discovers it never set anything aside — because nothing in the accounts ever asked it to. Depreciation records the using-up. Funding the replacement is a separate decision that somebody has to make deliberately.

WATCH-OUT: When comparing two branches, check they depreciate on the same basis. A branch charged for its building while another operates rent-free from a group property is not being compared like for like, and the difference can be larger than the profits being compared.

checks.q: ₦24m of vehicles over five years. The monthly depreciation charge is:
checks.why: ₦24m ÷ 5 years = ₦4.8m a year, ₦400,000 a month. The cost is spread over the period of use.

checks.q: Profit is ₦2m and depreciation ₦3m. Cash generated by trading is roughly:
checks.why: No money left the business for depreciation, so it is added back. This is why the cash flow statement begins with profit and adds it.

checks.q: Depreciation charged each month means the business is:
opts: Recording the asset being used up, with no money moving
Reducing its tax bill in cash
Setting money aside to replace the asset
checks.why: Nothing is saved and nothing is paid. The cash left when the asset was bought.

lessons.title: The lines that carry judgement
lessons.html:
Most of the P&L is arithmetic. A handful of lines are opinions, and knowing which is which is what separates a manager who reads accounts from one who merely receives them.

Accruals. Costs incurred but not yet invoiced. December's electricity, consumed in December, billed in January, belongs in December. Somebody has to estimate it. An accrual set too low flatters this month and punishes next.

Prepayments. The mirror image. A year's insurance paid in advance is not a cost of the month it was paid; eleven twelfths of it belongs to future months and sits on the balance sheet until then.

Provisions. An estimate of something expected but not certain — that a portion of receivables will not be collected, that a warranty will be claimed, that a dispute will be lost. Provisions are the most judgement-heavy line on the page, and the most useful to ask about.

Write-offs. The point at which an estimate becomes an admission: this stock is gone, this customer will not pay. Write-offs land in one month and describe deterioration that usually happened over many.

Why a manager should care about someone else's estimates. Because they move your reported result and they are not neutral. Consider a business under pressure to hit a number: raising the useful life of assets, thinning the bad debt provision, or deferring a write-off each improve this month's profit without anything improving in the business. None is fraud. All are judgement, and all are borrowed from next month.

The pattern worth watching is a P&L that meets its target every month by a small margin while receivables age and stock grows. That combination — steady reported profit, deteriorating balance sheet — is the signature of a result being managed rather than earned, and it is visible only if you read the two statements together.

The question to ask, and it is a fair one. "What changed in the estimates this month?" A finance team with nothing to hide will answer it in a sentence. It is not an accusation; it is the same question they ask each other.

The reverse also happens and is worth naming. A business having a strong month sometimes takes the opportunity to be prudent: raising provisions, writing off what it has been carrying, shortening asset lives. This depresses a good result to build cushion for a weaker one. It is not dishonest either, but it means an unusually poor month can follow an unusually good one for reasons that have nothing to do with trading. Estimates smooth results in both directions.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: A large write-off is rarely news about the month it appears in. When one lands, the useful question is not "why this month" but "how long was this true before anybody wrote it down" — because that is the number that tells you whether your reporting is working.

checks.q: December's electricity is consumed in December and billed in January. It belongs in:
checks.why: Costs belong to the period that consumed them. Somebody estimates the amount and accrues it.

checks.q: A year's insurance paid in advance in January is:
opts: Spread across the year, with the balance held as a prepayment
checks.why: Only the month's share is a cost; the rest sits on the balance sheet until its month arrives.

checks.q: Steady reported profit alongside ageing receivables and growing stock suggests:
opts: A result being managed rather than earned
checks.why: That combination is the classic signature, and it is visible only by reading the P&L and balance sheet together.

lessons.title: Reading a branch or department P&L
lessons.html:
Everything so far applies to a whole business. Most managers are handed something narrower: a branch, a department, a category. Those carry two complications that a group P&L does not, and both are worth understanding before you defend or attack a number.

Allocated overheads. Head office costs — the MD, finance, IT, the group insurance — have to land somewhere, and they are usually spread across units by some rule: share of revenue, of headcount, of floor space. The rule is a choice, and it is not neutral.

A branch allocated overhead on revenue is penalised for growing. A branch allocated on headcount is penalised for being labour-intensive. Neither reflects what head office actually did for that branch, and both change the branch's apparent profit without anything changing in the branch.

So the first question about any branch P&L is which costs the branch controls. If a manager cannot influence a line, holding them to it teaches them the numbers are unfair — and a manager who believes that stops reading them, which is a worse outcome than any allocation error.

The useful reading is two-stage. Start with controllable profit: branch revenue, cost of sales, and only the costs the branch decides — staff, local marketing, consumables, waste. That is the manager's scorecard. Then take allocated overhead off to reach the branch's contribution to the group. That is the investment scorecard: whether this branch should exist.

Those two questions have different answers surprisingly often. A branch can be well run and still not worth keeping; a branch can be poorly run and worth fixing rather than closing. Collapsing both into one number loses the distinction and usually leads to closing the wrong branch.

Transfer prices. Where stock moves between units at an internal price, that price sets each unit's margin — and it was decided by somebody, not by a market. A distribution centre charging branches a high internal price makes itself look profitable and the branches look weak. Nothing about the group changed.

What to do with all this. When a branch P&L looks wrong, check the allocation basis and the transfer price before you check the manager. Those two lines explain more surprising branch results than performance does.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Ask for your branch P&L with the allocated costs shown separately rather than buried in the expense lines. Any competent finance team can produce it that way, and it turns an argument about fairness into a conversation about performance.

Watch for costs that are allocated but avoidable. A branch charged ₦900,000 a month of head office overhead is not saving ₦900,000 if it closes — most of that cost stays and is simply redistributed to the branches that remain. Closing a branch on the strength of an allocated loss frequently makes the group worse off, because the contribution disappears and the overhead does not. Ask what would actually stop being spent.

checks.q: Head office overhead allocated to branches on share of revenue means:
opts: A growing branch is charged more for growing
checks.why: The basis is a choice with consequences. Allocating on revenue penalises exactly the branches doing best.

checks.q: Controllable profit for a branch manager should exclude:
checks.why: A manager cannot influence it. Holding them to it teaches them the numbers are unfair, and they stop reading them.

checks.q: A distribution centre raises its internal transfer price to branches. Group profit:
opts: Is unchanged — it moves between units
checks.why: Nothing entered or left the group. Only the apparent performance of each unit moved.

lessons.title: Six questions to ask about any P&L
lessons.html:
This chapter is the one to keep. Everything else explained how the statement works; these are the questions that turn it into a decision, in the order worth asking them.

1. What period is this, and what is it being compared to? A month against the same month last year is a real comparison. A month against last month compares a 28-day February with a 31-day January and a festive December with a flat one. A part-month against a full month is not a comparison at all, though it is presented as one constantly.

2. Which way did gross margin move, and why? Not gross profit in naira — the percentage. If it moved, you are looking at price, buying cost, mix, or loss, and the four have entirely different remedies. This single question surfaces more real problems than the rest of the P&L combined.

3. Are operating costs growing faster than revenue? Read them as a percentage of revenue rather than in naira. A cost base rising as a share of revenue is a business whose overhead is outgrowing its trading, and it is the slowest and most dangerous drift on the page because no single month looks alarming.

4. What is in the lines I cannot see inside? Anything vaguely named and large — sundry, general, other. Uncontrolled spending accumulates where nobody owns the label.

5. What changed in the estimates? Accruals, provisions, useful lives, write-offs. Not an accusation, just the question that stops a managed result passing as an earned one.

6. Does this profit look like cash? Profit rising while the bank falls is normal in a growing business — stock and receivables absorb the money. It is also what a serious problem looks like in its early months. The P&L cannot tell you which; it can only tell you to go and look at the other two statements, which is where the next chapters of this track go.

A discipline that costs nothing. Write your answer to question two before you open any other report. If you cannot answer it, you have not read the P&L — you have looked at it. The difference shows up in the meeting.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Six questions, ten minutes, once a month, in the same order. Managers who do this consistently spot problems roughly a quarter before those who read the numbers only when something already looks wrong — because by then the cause is usually three months old.

And one question deliberately not on the list: "did we hit budget?" It is the question most often asked first, and it is the least informative, because a budget is a forecast somebody made months ago under different conditions. Missing a bad budget is not failure and beating an easy one is not success. Ask what the numbers say about the business first, and only then ask what was expected of them.

checks.q: Comparing this month against last month is weak mainly because:
checks.why: A 28-day February against a 31-day January, or a flat month against a festive one, produces a difference that means nothing.

checks.q: The single most informative question about a P&L is:
opts: Which way gross margin moved, and why
checks.why: Margin describes the health of the trading itself, and its four causes each need a different response.

checks.q: Profit is rising while the bank balance falls. This is:
opts: Either — the P&L cannot tell you which, and you must look further
checks.why: Stock and receivables absorb cash in a growing business, and the early months of a serious problem look identical. Only the other statements distinguish them.

questions.q: Goods are delivered on 28 March and paid for on 30 April. Revenue is recognised in:
opts: Whichever month the customer's order was placed
questions.why: Revenue follows delivery, not collection.

questions.q: A customer's ₦1.5m advance payment for next month's goods appears this month as:
questions.why: You are holding their money until you deliver.

questions.q: A 10% trade discount on ₦2m of goods is recorded as:
opts: ₦2m revenue and ₦200,000 in cost of sales
questions.why: Discounts reduce the top line, which is why discounting hides inside revenue rather than announcing itself.

questions.q: VAT charged to customers is:
opts: Collected on behalf of the tax authority, not revenue
questions.why: It was never yours. Revenue stated inclusive of VAT overstates the business by 7.5%.

questions.q: Revenue rose sharply this month with no change in demand. The likeliest explanation is:
opts: A large delivery falling either side of month-end
A change in the VAT rate
questions.why: Delivery timing moves the top line without anything changing in trading.

questions.q: Purchasing ₦10m of stock that remains unsold affects this month's profit by:
questions.why: Cash became inventory. Cost reaches the P&L only on sale.

questions.why: The test is whether the cost was incurred to get the goods ready to sell.

questions.q: Closing stock is understated by ₦1m. The effect on reported profit is:
questions.why: Understated closing stock overstates cost of sales by the same amount, depressing profit.

questions.why: 17.5 ÷ 50 = 35%. The naira figure is gross profit; the percentage is margin.

questions.q: Cost ₦800, selling price ₦1,000. The margin is:
questions.why: 200 ÷ 1,000 = 20%. The 25% figure is markup on cost.

questions.q: Pricing for a 40% margin by adding 40% to cost actually achieves:
questions.why: Adding 40% to cost gives a 28.6% margin. This confusion is expensive and common.

opts: No effect until the goods are paid for
Margin lost that selling effort cannot recover
questions.why: Buying price is one of the four movers of margin, and currency is the one nobody in the branch controls.

questions.why: Mix is about what you sell proportionally more of, so the remedy is what you promote and stock.

questions.q: Gross margin has fallen two points with no price or supplier change. Look first at:
opts: Stock: count quality, cut-off and unrecorded write-offs

questions.q: A second supervisor needed once a shop passes a certain size is an example of:
questions.why: Step costs hold flat then jump, which is why they surprise people.

questions.q: Fixed cost ₦3m a month, gross margin 40%. Revenue needed to break even is:
Operating expenses are best compared against:

questions.q: A large and vaguely named expense category matters because:
opts: It is where uncontrolled spending accumulates unowned
It must be reallocated to cost of sales
questions.why: A line nobody owns is a line nobody questions.

questions.q: A branch failing to cover its fixed base should first establish:
opts: Whether the gap is a revenue problem or a cost problem
questions.why: Cutting the people who generate revenue turns a slow decline into a fast one.

questions.q: Operating profit deliberately excludes:
questions.why: Financing and tax are not the operating manager's doing, so the line answers whether the trading works.

questions.q: Two units make identical operating profit; one carries heavy interest. This tells you:
opts: They traded identically and are financed differently
One has higher costs of sale
questions.why: Interest is a financing decision made above the unit.

questions.q: Strong operating profit with negative net profit indicates:
questions.why: Selling harder will not fix the cost of debt.

questions.q: The tax charge in the accounts and the tax paid in cash that period are:
opts: Rarely equal — different bases and timing

questions.why: In a business carrying debt the gap can be most of the number, and two people can be certain and opposed.

questions.q: ₦30m of equipment over six years produces an annual depreciation charge of:
questions.why: ₦30m ÷ 6 = ₦5m a year.

questions.why: Depreciation is added back because no money moved when it was charged.

questions.q: Extending the assumed useful life of assets from three years to five:
opts: Increases reported profit without anything changing in the business
questions.why: It is judgement, entirely legitimate, and one of the quietest ways to improve a number.

questions.q: Depreciation charged each month means the business:
opts: Is saving to replace the asset
Is recording use with no money moving
questions.why: Nothing is set aside, which is why a profitable company can be unable to afford replacements.

opts: Makes the comparison unlike for like, possibly by more than the profits compared
questions.why: Check the basis before comparing units on profit.

questions.q: An estimate of receivables not expected to be collected is:
questions.why: A provision is expected but not certain, which makes it the most judgement-heavy line on the page.

questions.q: Thinning the bad debt provision to help hit a target is:
opts: Judgement that borrows from next month
questions.why: It improves this month's profit without anything improving in the business.

questions.q: A year's rent paid in advance sits on the balance sheet as:
questions.why: Only the month's share is a cost; the rest belongs to future months.

opts: How long it was true before anybody wrote it down
questions.why: That answer tells you whether your reporting is working, which matters more than the amount.

questions.q: Allocating head office cost on share of revenue means:

questions.why: Holding a manager to a line they cannot influence teaches them the numbers are unfair.

opts: Reading controllable profit and contribution separately

read_bs.title: Reading the Balance Sheet
read_bs.desc: What the business is standing on, and where it is exposed. Working capital, stock days, debtor and creditor days, the cash cycle, what net book value really means, and the six questions that turn a position into a decision. Worked in naira on trading numbers.

lessons.title: What you own, what you owe, and what is left
lessons.html:
The profit and loss account covers a period: what happened between the first of the month and the last. The balance sheet is different in kind. It is a photograph taken at one instant — the close of business on the last day — showing what the business owns, what it owes, and the difference between the two.

That difference is what belongs to the owners, and it is the only number on the page that nobody chooses directly. It falls out of the other two.

Three blocks, and that is the whole structure.

Assets are things of value the business controls: cash in the bank, stock on the shelves, money customers owe you, vehicles, fittings, the building if you own it.

Liabilities are obligations to other people: suppliers awaiting payment, a bank loan, tax owed, staff salaries accrued but not yet paid, a customer's deposit for goods you have not delivered.

Equity is what remains: assets less liabilities. It is the owners' stake — what would be left in theory if everything were sold at book value and every debt settled.

Why a manager should care about a statement they will never prepare. Because the P&L can only tell you half the story, and the more comfortable half. A business can report a profit every month for two years while its stock swells, its customers stop paying and its supplier terms quietly stretch. Every one of those developments is invisible on the P&L and unmistakable on the balance sheet.

The two statements are also linked, tightly. The profit you earned this month arrives on the balance sheet as an increase in equity. If a business made ₦8,000,000 profit and took nothing out, equity rose ₦8,000,000. Where it went — into stock, into receivables, into the bank, into repaying a loan — is what the balance sheet tells you and the P&L cannot.

The instant matters more than people expect. Because it is a photograph, a balance sheet can be dressed for the picture. Paying suppliers on the 2nd rather than the 30th, or pushing a delivery over month-end, changes what the statement shows without changing anything real about the business. This is not usually sinister; it is just worth knowing that a single balance sheet is a moment, and a trend of them is evidence.

What good reading looks like. Nobody sensible reads a balance sheet top to bottom. You read it for change: what is bigger than last quarter, what is smaller, and what that movement says about where the money went. A manager who can do that in ten minutes is doing something most people in the building cannot.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Always read a balance sheet next to the previous one. A single column tells you the position; two columns tell you the direction, and direction is what you can act on.

One warning about the word "worth". Equity is not what the business would sell for. It is assets at book value less liabilities, and book value is history — what was paid, less what has been charged since. A business with a well-known name, a trained team and a loyal customer base carries none of that on the page, while a business with obsolete stock carries it at cost until somebody writes it down. Equity is a useful number and a poor valuation.

checks.q: A balance sheet describes:
opts: A single moment — the close of the last day
checks.why: The P&L covers a period; the balance sheet is a photograph at one instant, which is why a single one is a moment and a series is evidence.

checks.q: A business made ₦8m profit and distributed nothing. On the balance sheet:
checks.why: Profit arrives as an increase in equity. Where the money actually went — stock, receivables, bank, debt repayment — is the interesting part.

checks.q: Paying suppliers on the 2nd instead of the 30th changes:
checks.why: It is a moment, and moments can be dressed. Usually not sinister, but a reason to read the trend rather than one column.

lessons.title: The accounting equation as an idea, not a formula
lessons.html:
Assets equal liabilities plus equity. It is stated as a formula, which makes it look like arithmetic to be memorised. It is better understood as a sentence about the world: everything the business has, somebody has a claim on.

Either an outsider has the claim — a supplier, a lender, the tax authority — or the owners do. There is no third possibility, which is why the two sides can never disagree.

Follow one transaction and it stops being abstract.

You buy ₦5,000,000 of stock on credit. Assets rise ₦5,000,000, because you now hold the stock. Liabilities rise ₦5,000,000, because the supplier is owed. Equity does not move — you are no better or worse off, you are simply larger on both sides. This is why buying stock does not make you richer, however much fuller the warehouse looks.

Now you sell that stock for ₦7,000,000 cash. Cash rises ₦7,000,000, stock falls ₦5,000,000, so assets rise ₦2,000,000 net. Liabilities are unchanged. Equity therefore rises ₦2,000,000 — and that ₦2,000,000 is exactly the gross profit the P&L reported. The two statements agreed without anybody making them agree.

Now the transaction that catches people out. You pay the supplier the ₦5,000,000. Cash falls, so assets fall ₦5,000,000. Liabilities fall ₦5,000,000. Equity does not move at all — and neither does profit. Paying a bill is not a cost. The cost happened when the goods were sold; paying is settlement.

That single point resolves most of the confusion managers have about why the bank balance and the profit figure refuse to agree.

The one place equity moves without profit. When owners put money in, or take money out. An owner injecting ₦10,000,000 raises cash and raises equity, and no profit was earned. An owner drawing ₦3,000,000 reduces both, and no loss was made. Drawings are not an expense, and a business that treats them as one will understate its own performance.

Why this is worth twenty minutes of your life. Because once you can trace a transaction through both sides, you stop needing to be told what a balance sheet movement means — you can work it out. Stock up and payables up is buying on credit. Stock up and cash down is buying with your own money. The same increase in stock, two completely different stories, and the balance sheet distinguishes them where the P&L shows neither.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: When any balance sheet number moves and you want to know what happened, ask which other number moved with it. Assets and liabilities together means an outsider funded it. Assets and equity together means you earned it or the owners put it in.

A note on why this never fails to balance. Every transaction touches at least two places, and always in a way that preserves the equation. That is the whole of double-entry, and it is why a balance sheet that does not balance is not a business problem but a bookkeeping one. What it does not guarantee is that the numbers are right — a balance sheet balances perfectly well with the wrong stock figure in it, because the error simply appears on both sides.

checks.q: You buy ₦5m of stock on credit. Equity:
checks.why: Assets and liabilities both rise. You are larger on both sides and no better off — which is why a full warehouse is not wealth.

checks.q: You pay a supplier ₦5m you already owed. Profit:
opts: Is unaffected — the cost occurred when the goods were sold
checks.why: Paying a bill is settlement, not cost. This one point resolves most confusion about why cash and profit disagree.

checks.q: Stock rose and payables rose by the same amount. This tells you:
opts: The stock was bought on supplier credit
checks.why: Assets and liabilities moving together means an outsider funded the increase.

lessons.title: Current and non-current, and why the split matters
lessons.html:
Both assets and liabilities are split in two, and the dividing line is time: within twelve months, or beyond.

Current assets are cash or things expected to become cash within a year: bank balances, stock, money owed by customers, prepayments.

Non-current assets are held to be used rather than sold: vehicles, equipment, fittings, buildings, software.

Current liabilities fall due within a year: suppliers, tax, accrued salaries, the next twelve months of a loan.

Non-current liabilities fall due later: the rest of that loan, long leases.

The split exists to answer one question: can this business pay what is about to fall due? Nothing else on the balance sheet answers it, and it is the question that determines whether a business survives the next quarter regardless of how profitable it is.

Working capital is current assets less current liabilities. Current assets of ₦46,000,000 against current liabilities of ₦31,000,000 gives ₦15,000,000 of working capital, and a current ratio of 1.5. A ratio below 1 means the things falling due within the year exceed the things becoming cash within the year — which does not guarantee failure, but does mean the business is relying on something not yet on the page.

Where the crude reading goes wrong, and it matters. Not all current assets are equally current. Cash is cash. Receivables become cash when customers pay, which for a distributor with slow debtors may be ninety days. Stock becomes cash only after it is sold and then collected — and slow-moving stock may never become cash at all.

So a business with a comfortable current ratio built almost entirely from stock is not comfortable. The quick ratio — current assets excluding stock, over current liabilities — asks the harder question: if nothing else sold from today, could we meet what falls due? For a stock-heavy retailer the two ratios can differ enormously, and the second is the honest one.

The trap on the liability side. The current portion of a long-term loan sits in current liabilities, and people reading quickly treat the loan as long-term because that is how they think of it. The twelve months of instalments ahead are due within twelve months, and the business must find them from somewhere.

WATCH-OUT: A rising current ratio is not automatically good news. If it is rising because stock is piling up and customers are paying more slowly, the ratio is improving while the business gets weaker. Always ask which component moved.

Where the twelve-month rule gets interesting. Stock that will not sell within a year is still shown as current, because that is the convention for the category rather than a judgement about the item. So a business sitting on dead stock reports it among the assets expected to become cash within twelve months, and the ratio inherits the optimism. This is another reason the ageing profile matters more than the classification.

checks.q: The line dividing current from non-current is:
opts: Whether it was bought on credit
checks.why: Current means expected to become cash, or to fall due, within a year.

checks.q: Current assets ₦46m, current liabilities ₦31m. The current ratio is:
checks.why: 46 ÷ 31 ≈ 1.5. Working capital is the ₦15m difference; the ratio is the relationship.

checks.q: A comfortable current ratio made up almost entirely of stock is:
opts: Weaker than it looks — stock becomes cash only after it sells and is collected
checks.why: The quick ratio strips stock out and asks the harder question, which for a stock-heavy retailer is the honest one.

lessons.title: Inventory: the number that moves your margin
lessons.html:
For a retail or distribution business, stock is usually the largest current asset and the one most capable of misleading. It is also the point where the balance sheet and the P&L are joined at the hip — which is why an error here damages both statements at once.

Stock is carried at cost, not at what you hope to sell it for. ₦30,000,000 of stock means ₦30,000,000 was spent acquiring and preparing it. The profit is recognised when it sells, not when it arrives.

The exception matters: if stock is worth less than it cost — damaged, expired, obsolete, superseded — it must be written down to what it will actually fetch. Accounts may never carry stock above its recoverable value. That rule is what turns a slow-moving line into a P&L event, eventually.

The joint that makes this chapter important. As module 2 showed, cost of sales is opening stock plus purchases less closing stock. Closing stock is a balance sheet number. So every naira of error in the stock figure is a naira of error in profit, in the opposite direction.

Count ₦2,000,000 too much and cost of sales is ₦2,000,000 too low, profit ₦2,000,000 too high, and the balance sheet ₦2,000,000 too strong. One mistake, two wrong statements, and nothing anywhere flags it.

This is why the stock count is not an inventory chore. It is the single largest determinant of whether your accounts are true.

What to look at, beyond the number. Stock rising faster than sales is the classic warning: money converting into goods faster than goods convert into money. Measure it as stock days — stock divided by cost of sales, times 365. Stock of ₦30,000,000 on cost of sales of ₦180,000,000 is 61 days. If that was 45 days a year ago, roughly ₦8,000,000 of cash has quietly moved onto the shelves.

Ageing beats totals. A stable total can hide a rotting composition: fast lines thinning while dead stock accumulates underneath. Ask for stock by age, and treat anything older than a defined threshold as a decision waiting to be made rather than an asset.

And the quiet one. A business that never writes anything off is not a business with no obsolete stock — it is a business not looking. Zero write-offs year after year is a finding, not a clean bill of health.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Two numbers, monthly, on one line: stock days and the value of stock older than your threshold. Almost everything that goes wrong with inventory shows up in one of them long before it shows up in profit.

One thing that flatters stock quietly. Goods held on consignment, or bought under an arrangement where they can be returned, may sit on your shelves without being yours. Conversely, stock you own may sit in a customer's warehouse. The physical location and the accounting ownership are different questions, and businesses that count what they can see rather than what they own get both the stock figure and the cost of sales wrong.

checks.q: Stock is carried on the balance sheet at:
opts: Cost, unless it is worth less than cost
checks.why: Profit is recognised when it sells. Stock worth less than cost must be written down.

checks.q: Stock ₦30m, cost of sales ₦180m. Stock days are roughly:
checks.why: 30 ÷ 180 × 365 ≈ 61 days. Rising stock days means cash converting into goods faster than goods convert into cash.

checks.q: A business reporting zero stock write-offs for three years is most likely:
checks.why: Every stockholding business has obsolescence. Zero write-offs is a finding rather than a clean bill of health.

lessons.title: Receivables: revenue you have not been paid for
lessons.html:
Receivables — debtors — are sales you have made and not yet collected. As module 2 established, the sale became revenue on delivery. The balance sheet is where the unpaid consequence sits, and it grows quietly while the P&L looks healthy.

The measure that matters is time, not size. Debtor days: receivables divided by revenue, times 365. Receivables of ₦24,000,000 on revenue of ₦146,000,000 is about 60 days. Whether that is good depends entirely on your terms — 60 days against 30-day terms means half your customers are late, and the business is financing them.

That phrase is worth sitting with. You are financing your customers. Every naira in receivables is a naira you have spent on goods and not recovered. A distributor with ₦24,000,000 out has, in effect, lent that to its customers interest-free — and may itself be paying interest on an overdraft to do it.

Ageing is where the truth is. A total tells you almost nothing; the split tells you everything. ₦24,000,000 made up of ₦20,000,000 under thirty days and ₦4,000,000 over ninety is a healthy book with a small problem. The same ₦24,000,000 made up of ₦9,000,000 current and ₦15,000,000 over ninety is a serious one dressed as an ordinary one.

Debt over ninety days rarely improves with age. The probability of collection falls steeply, and every month of delay makes the conversation harder and the customer less willing.

The provision, and what it admits. Because some receivables will not be collected, accounts carry a provision for doubtful debts, which reduces the asset and reduces profit. It is an estimate, and as module 2's chapter on judgement noted, it is a favourite place to flatter a result. A provision that stays flat while the ageing deteriorates is not prudence; it is postponement.

Concentration is the risk nobody measures. Ask what share of receivables sits with the largest customer. If one name is 40% of the book, that customer's difficulty is your difficulty, and it will arrive without warning. A well-spread book of the same size is a materially different exposure.

What a manager should actually do. Read the ageing monthly, not the total. Chase at the point the invoice becomes overdue rather than when it becomes alarming. And treat a customer who is slow but growing as a decision rather than a success — more sales to somebody who does not pay makes the position worse, not better.

A distinction worth keeping clear. A customer who disputes an invoice is not the same as a customer who cannot pay, and both sit in the same ageing bucket. Disputes are usually a service or paperwork failure on your side — a wrong price, a short delivery, a missing document — and they are fixable in days by somebody with authority. Grouping them with genuine credit problems means the fixable ones age alongside the unfixable, and nobody separates them until the total is alarming.

WATCH-OUT: Revenue growth and receivables growth arriving together, with receivables growing faster, is one of the most reliable early warnings in business. It usually means terms are being stretched to win the sales — and the sales are real while the cash is not.

checks.q: Receivables ₦24m on revenue ₦146m gives debtor days of roughly:
checks.why: 24 ÷ 146 × 365 ≈ 60 days. Against 30-day terms that means the business is financing its customers.

checks.q: ₦24m of receivables: which composition is the serious problem?
checks.why: Age, not size, carries the meaning. Debt over ninety days rarely improves with age.

checks.q: Revenue growing while receivables grow faster usually means:
opts: Terms are being stretched to win the sales
checks.why: The sales are real; the cash is not. It is one of the most reliable early warnings there is.

lessons.title: Payables: the money you are holding
lessons.html:
Payables — creditors — are what you owe suppliers for goods and services already received. It is the mirror of receivables, and the only large balance sheet line where bigger can be better.

Supplier credit is free funding, and it is the cheapest a business will ever get. If a supplier lets you pay in thirty days, they have financed your stock for thirty days at no interest. Every day of supplier credit is a day you do not need an overdraft.

Creditor days measure it: payables divided by cost of sales, times 365. Payables of ₦27,000,000 on cost of sales of ₦180,000,000 is about 55 days.

Put the three together and you have the cash cycle. Stock days plus debtor days less creditor days. On our numbers: 61 + 60 − 55 = 66 days. That is how long the business funds its own trading before the money comes back — and it is the number that determines how much cash growth will consume.

Because that is the counter-intuitive part: growth eats cash. If every ₦1,000,000 of extra monthly sales requires 66 days of funding, doubling sales does not double comfort. It doubles the hole to be funded, and profitable businesses fail this way far more often than unprofitable ones fail from losses.

But payables have a limit, and it is not the terms. It is the relationship. Stretching suppliers works until it does not: supply gets slower, priority goes elsewhere, prices harden, and eventually deliveries stop at the moment you most need them. Rising creditor days can mean sharp treasury management or a business quietly running out of money, and the balance sheet cannot tell you which. The supplier can.

Watch for the tell. Creditor days rising while cash falls and receivables lengthen is not treasury policy. It is a business paying late because it cannot pay on time, and the three moving together is the signature.

One number that hides here. Payables often include accrued expenses and tax not yet remitted. Tax collected and not yet paid over is not working capital, however much it looks like it — it is somebody else's money sitting in your account with a due date attached. Businesses that fund operations from it discover the cost when the due date arrives.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Track the cash cycle as one monthly number. A business improving margin while its cash cycle lengthens is not necessarily improving, and the two facts sit in different statements — so nobody notices unless somebody puts them side by side.

The other direction is worth naming too. Paying suppliers faster than you need to is not virtue; it is lending them your money. If a supplier offers thirty days and you pay in ten, you have funded twenty days of their business out of your own working capital for nothing in return. Unless there is a settlement discount that beats your cost of money, take the terms you were given — that is what they are for.

checks.q: Payables ₦27m on cost of sales ₦180m gives creditor days of roughly:
checks.why: 27 ÷ 180 × 365 ≈ 55 days. Every day of supplier credit is a day you do not need an overdraft.

checks.q: Stock days 61, debtor days 60, creditor days 55. The cash cycle is:
checks.why: 61 + 60 − 55 = 66 days of self-funded trading. It is what determines how much cash growth will consume.

checks.q: Creditor days rising, cash falling, receivables lengthening together indicates:
opts: A business paying late because it cannot pay on time
checks.why: Either reading is possible for creditor days alone. All three moving together is the signature of trouble.

lessons.title: Fixed assets, and the balance sheet that ages
lessons.html:
Non-current assets — property, vehicles, equipment, fittings, software — are held to be used rather than sold, and they are the part of the balance sheet most likely to be quietly wrong.

Two numbers, and the gap between them is the point. Cost is what you paid. Accumulated depreciation is how much has been charged against profit since. The difference, net book value, is what appears on the balance sheet.

Vehicles at ₦24,000,000 cost with ₦19,200,000 accumulated depreciation show ₦4,800,000 net. That does not mean they are worth ₦4,800,000. It means ₦4,800,000 of the original cost has yet to be charged to profit. Net book value is an unexpired cost, not a valuation, and treating it as one is the commonest error in reading this section.

Read the ratio, not the number. Net book value against cost tells you how used-up the asset base is. ₦4,800,000 against ₦24,000,000 means the fleet is 80% depreciated — old, near replacement, and about to demand cash that nothing in the accounts has set aside. A business with heavily depreciated assets and a healthy profit is often a business with an unfunded replacement bill approaching.

Additions and disposals tell the story of intent. Rising fixed assets means the business is investing. Falling means it is not replacing, which may be prudence in a downturn or may be a business slowly consuming its own capacity. The balance sheet shows which is happening; only management can say which was intended.

Revaluation, where property is involved. Some businesses revalue land and buildings upward, which raises assets and raises equity through a reserve rather than through profit. Nothing was earned and no cash arrived. It can materially change how strong a balance sheet looks, so when equity jumps, check whether the business earned it or revalued it.

The asset that is not there. Leased premises, leased vehicles, rented equipment — depending on treatment these may not appear as assets at all, while the obligation to pay for them is entirely real. Two businesses operating identically, one owning and one leasing, present very different balance sheets. Comparing them on asset totals compares financing choices rather than operations.

WATCH-OUT: A large "assets under construction" or "capital work in progress" balance that does not move for several periods is worth asking about. It is where stalled projects sit, unfinished and undepreciated, and it can hold real money doing nothing while looking like an asset.

And one practical check. Ask whether the fixed asset register has been walked recently — whether somebody has physically confirmed the assets still exist and are still in use. Registers accumulate items that were scrapped, stolen or replaced years ago, and every one of those is carrying a book value and a depreciation charge for something that is not there. It is unglamorous work and it is the only way the number becomes trustworthy.

checks.q: Vehicles: cost ₦24m, accumulated depreciation ₦19.2m. Net book value means:
opts: ₦4.8m of the original cost has yet to be charged to profit
checks.why: Net book value is an unexpired cost, not a valuation. Treating it as market value is the commonest error here.

checks.q: A fleet 80% depreciated with healthy profit most likely indicates:
checks.why: Depreciation records use; it sets nothing aside. The replacement has to be funded separately.

checks.q: Equity rose sharply with no corresponding profit. A likely explanation is:
opts: A property revaluation or owner injection
checks.why: Revaluation raises assets and equity through a reserve. Nothing was earned and no cash arrived.

lessons.title: Equity: what the owners actually have
lessons.html:
Equity is the residual — assets less liabilities — and it is usually shown in parts, each of which answers a different question about where the owners' stake came from.

Share capital, or capital introduced, is what the owners put in. It rises only when they put in more.

Retained earnings are every naira of profit the business has ever made and not distributed, accumulated since it began. This is the line that connects the two statements permanently: each period's profit lands here, each dividend or drawing leaves from here.

Reserves cover amounts set aside for particular reasons — a revaluation reserve being the common one.

The most useful thing this section tells you is how the business was built. Equity of ₦120,000,000 made up of ₦100,000,000 introduced and ₦20,000,000 retained is a business funded largely by its owners. The same ₦120,000,000 made up of ₦10,000,000 introduced and ₦110,000,000 retained is a business that funded itself out of its own trading. Both look identical on the total; they are entirely different animals.

Negative retained earnings — accumulated losses — mean the business has lost more since inception than it has made. It can still be trading perfectly well today; the line is history, not a verdict on the present. But it does mean any current profit is repairing past damage before it builds anything.

Drawings and dividends are the line to watch closely in an owner-managed business. They are not costs and never appear on the P&L, so a business can report healthy profit every year while the owners extract more than it earns, and equity falls steadily. The P&L will look fine throughout. Only the balance sheet shows the business getting weaker — which is precisely why an owner reading only the P&L can be surprised by their own bank.

Gearing, in one sentence. Compare debt to equity. A business with ₦80,000,000 of borrowings against ₦40,000,000 of equity is carrying twice as much of other people's money as its own, which magnifies both good years and bad ones. There is no correct level, but there is a level at which a poor quarter stops being uncomfortable and starts being existential.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Equity movement over a year is one of the fastest health checks available. Rising equity with no owner injection means the business earned it. Falling equity with profit reported means it is being taken out faster than it is being made.

Why gearing is a temperament question as much as a financial one. Debt magnifies. A geared business in a good year returns more to its owners than an ungeared one, because the lenders take a fixed amount and the owners keep the rest. In a bad year the lenders still take their fixed amount, and the owners absorb the whole shortfall. The right level therefore depends on how volatile your trading is and how much of a bad year you could absorb without the question becoming existential — not on what a ratio table says is normal.

lessons.title: Reading a balance sheet as an exposure map
lessons.html:
This is the chapter to keep. The balance sheet is not a scorecard — it does not tell you how well you did. It tells you what you are standing on and where you are exposed, which is a more useful thing to know and a harder one to get from anywhere else.

Six questions, in order.

1. Where did the money go? Compare against the prior period. Equity up ₦8,000,000 from profit, but cash down ₦2,000,000 — so ₦10,000,000 went somewhere. Stock and receivables are almost always the answer, and finding which one is the whole exercise.

2. Can we pay what is about to fall due? Current assets against current liabilities, and then the same excluding stock. If the second answer is uncomfortable, the first was flattering you.

3. How long is the cash cycle, and is it lengthening? Stock days plus debtor days less creditor days. A lengthening cycle means growth will consume more cash than it did last year, which is the thing that catches profitable businesses out.

4. What is the shape of the receivables book? Not the total — the ageing, and the concentration. One customer at 40% is a different business from a well-spread book of the same size.

5. How used-up are the assets? Net book value against cost. Heavy depreciation with no additions is a replacement bill forming quietly, and nothing has been set aside for it.

6. Who owns this business's future — the owners or the lenders? Debt against equity, and whether the trend is toward one or the other.

Read the two statements together or you will be misled by both. The P&L alone shows a profitable business that may be running out of money. The balance sheet alone shows a position without explaining how it arose. Profit rising while the cash cycle lengthens and receivables age is the single most common pattern in a business that is about to have a difficult year, and neither statement shows it on its own.

The discipline worth building. Ten minutes, quarterly, against the previous quarter, in the order above. Write down which number moved most and why. You will be right about the why perhaps half the time at first — but you will be asking the finance team a specific question rather than a vague one, and that alone changes the answer you get.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: If you take one habit from this module, make it question one. "Equity rose, cash fell, so where did the money go?" is the question that finds stock problems, collection problems and overtrading before any of them reach the P&L.

What this module does not tell you, and where it goes next. The balance sheet shows the position and the P&L shows the period, but neither actually traces the movement of cash — they only let you infer it. The statement that does that directly is the cash flow statement, and it is the subject of the next module. Between the three, the questions "did we do well", "what are we standing on" and "where did the money actually go" each have a proper home.
